title: Your AI Agent Says It's Finished. That's When the Work Starts.
dek: Everybody's selling cheaper intelligence. Nobody wants to talk about the cost of checking its work.
body: I keep hearing that AI is making software development cheaper. And maybe it is. But there's a question nobody seems particularly eager to answer: cheaper for whom?
The model provider? Absolutely. The guy paying the API bill? Probably. The engineer who has to figure out why the beautifully written code doesn't actually work? That's a different conversation.
You can generate an entire application in an afternoon now. Authentication, database, payment processing, admin dashboard. Ask nicely and the agent will even congratulate itself when it's finished.
Then you open the thing.

The login works until somebody resets a password. The payment page looks beautiful but doesn't handle a declined card. The database permissions are configured so generously that users can potentially read records belonging to other users.
And the agent says everything passed.
That's the part that interests me.
## Forty cents of intelligence, three hours of cleanup
Stanford's 2025 AI Index documented something remarkable: between November 2022 and October 2024, the cost of inference at approximately GPT-3.5-level performance fell more than 280-fold.
That's an extraordinary engineering achievement. It reflects improvements in hardware, algorithms, and model efficiency.
But inference cost is only one component of what it costs to get useful work out of these systems.
Imagine two coding agents.
One costs forty cents per attempt and finishes the task correctly 80 percent of the time. Another costs ninety cents and succeeds 96 percent of the time.
Those are hypothetical numbers, not vendor benchmarks.
If failures are independent and you can retry indefinitely, the cheaper model costs about fifty cents per successful completion in model fees. The expensive one costs roughly ninety-four cents.
Fine. Buy the cheaper model.
Except now somebody has to investigate the failures. If that takes an engineer fifteen minutes, the economics change immediately.
And retries aren't always independent. Sometimes the agent makes the same mistake repeatedly because it misunderstood the architecture in the first place.
You can't retry your way out of every bad assumption.
## The benchmark tells you what the model can do. Not what it will do.
Here's another thing.
A coding benchmark can tell you whether a model solved a particular collection of programming problems. That's useful.
It doesn't necessarily tell you whether the same model can spend six hours modifying a production application without quietly breaking something unrelated.
Those are different abilities.
Real software has dependencies, undocumented assumptions, aging libraries, deployment environments, and people who made questionable decisions five years ago.
A model can be brilliant at writing a function and terrible at understanding why changing that function breaks the rest of the application.
That's not an argument against AI coding. It's an argument for measuring the right thing.

I want to know how often an agent finishes a task without human intervention. How many defects survive its tests? How often does it introduce a security regression? How much engineering time does it actually eliminate?
And I want those numbers from production-like environments, not just carefully packaged benchmark exercises.
## Bigger isn't automatically better
The other obsession is model size.
For a genuinely difficult architectural problem, I'd rather have a capable frontier model working through the design than a tiny model confidently improvising.
But should that same frontier model spend its time changing button labels, formatting JSON, or writing routine database queries?
Probably not.
There are plenty of tasks where a smaller, specialized model is sufficient.
The interesting engineering problem is deciding which model gets which job, and when to escalate.

A good routing system should recognize when a task requires deeper reasoning, when the evidence is insufficient, and when the potential cost of a mistake justifies a more expensive model or human review.
That's a much more useful product than simply giving everybody access to the biggest model available.
## What I'd actually pay for
Give me an AI coding system that understands the repository, makes a controlled change, runs meaningful tests, checks authorization boundaries, and tells me exactly what it couldn't verify.
Don't tell me everything is perfect.
Tell me which tests ran. Tell me which files changed. Tell me whether the application was deployed. Tell me what might still be broken.
If it can't establish something, I want it to say so.
That kind of honesty isn't a personality feature. It's part of a reliable engineering system.
The companies that figure this out will have something considerably more valuable than another benchmark trophy.
They'll have software that people can actually trust to finish the job.
And I'll happily pay more than forty cents for that.
Editorial note: This is a technology opinion column. The cost comparison and software scenarios are illustrative, not the results of original testing.
